nodes.name: Reinforcement learning control problem
nodes.statement: At each time step $t$, the controller observes a state vector $x_t$, selects an action $a_t$, and receives a scalar reward $r_t$ from the environment. Find a control policy that maximises the expected discounted future sum of rewards (the $return$).

nodes.name: Reward, state and action
nodes.statement: In a reinforcement learning problem, at each time step $t$ the controller observes a state vector $x_t \in \mathcal{X}$, selects an action $a_t \in \mathcal{A}$, and receives a scalar reward (reinforcement) $r_t$ from the environment.
nodes.statement_clean: Defines the basic objects of a reinforcement learning interaction: state, action, reward.

nodes.name: Q-function (action-value function)
nodes.statement: The $Q$-value of a state-action pair is the predicted discounted return: $Q(x_t, a) = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k} \mid x_t,\, a_t = a\right]$, where $\gamma \in [0,1]$ is the $discount\ factor$.
nodes.statement_clean: Q(x,a) is the expected discounted return when taking action a in state x and following the policy thereafter.

nodes.name: Q-value definition (eq. 1)
nodes.statement: $Q(x_t, a) = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k} \mid x_t, a_t = a\right]$

nodes.name: Bellman recursion for Q (eq. 2)
nodes.statement: $Q(x_t, a_t) = \mathbb{E}\left[r_t + \gamma \max_b Q(x_{t+1}, b)\right]$

nodes.name: Convergence of one-step Q-learning (Watkins 1989)
nodes.statement: The one-step Q-learning rule with target $r_t + \gamma \max_b Q(x_{t+1}, b)$ has been shown to converge to the optimal $Q$-function for finite-state Markov decision problems when stored as a lookup table.
assumptions: All state-action pairs visited infinitely often
conclusions: Greedy policy with respect to converged $Q$ is optimal

nodes.name: One-step Q-learning update (eq. 3)
nodes.statement: $Q(x_t, a_t) \leftarrow Q(x_t, a_t) + \eta\, \Delta_t$, with $\Delta_t = r_t + \gamma \max_b Q(x_{t+1}, b) - Q(x_t, a_t)$.

nodes.name: Limits of exploratory actions
nodes.statement: Exploration is necessary because $Q$ cannot be learned by always choosing the action with the highest current $Q(x_t, a_t)$; otherwise other actions with lower current estimates may in fact be better. Selecting actions has a direct effect on the rate at which Q-learning converges.

nodes.name: Function-approximation Q-learning weight update (Sutton/Lin)
nodes.statement: When $Q$ is represented by a neural network with weights $w$, the weight update is $\Delta w_t = \eta\, \Delta_t\, \nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$, where $\nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$ is the gradient computed by back-propagation and $\eta$ is the learning rate.

nodes.name: Connectionist Q-learning weight update (eq. 4)
nodes.statement: $\Delta w_t = \eta\, \Delta_t\, \nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$, with $\Delta_t$ as in eq. 3.

nodes.name: TD($\lambda$) (Sutton 1988)
nodes.statement: $TD(\lambda)$ is a family of methods for learning predictions, in which earlier temporal differences are weighted by $0 \le \lambda \le 1$. It generalises one-step prediction-error learning by allowing credit to be assigned to states visited in the past.
nodes.origin_citation: Sutton 1988 (Learning to predict by the methods of temporal differences)

nodes.name: Eligibility trace
nodes.statement: The eligibility of a weight $w$ at time $t$ is a discounted sum of past output gradients: $e_t(w) = \sum_{k=0}^{t} (\gamma\lambda)^{t-k} \nabla_w Q(x_k, a_k)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Eligibility trace accumulates a $(\gamma\lambda)$-decayed sum of past gradients of Q with respect to weights.

nodes.name: Eligibility-trace weight update (eq. 5)
nodes.statement: $\Delta w_t = \eta\, \Delta_t\, e_t(w)$, where $e_t(w) = \sum_{k=0}^{t} (\gamma\lambda)^{t-k} \nabla_w Q(x_k, a_k)$.

nodes.name: Backward replay
nodes.statement: $Backward\ replay$ is the procedure in which state-action pairs encountered during a trial are stored, then presented to the learner in reverse temporal order so that prediction errors propagate correctly through the eligibility traces.

nodes.name: Watkins' Q($\lambda$)
nodes.statement: Watkins' Q($\lambda$) combines one-step Q-learning with eligibility traces, but cuts the trace whenever a non-greedy (exploratory) action is taken so that bootstrap targets remain consistent with the greedy policy.

nodes.name: Watkins' Q($\lambda$) TD error with cut-off (eq. 6)
nodes.statement: $\Delta_t' = r_t + \gamma \max_b Q(x_{t+1}, b) - \max_b Q(x_t, b)$. If the greedy action is taken at every step, this equation is exactly equivalent to standard $Q$-learning.

nodes.name: Q($\lambda$) of Peng and Williams
nodes.statement: Performs a normal one-step Q-learning update to improve $Q_{t-1}$, then uses temporal differences between successive greedy predictions to update from there, regardless of whether greedy actions are taken; thus traces need not be zeroed.

nodes.name: Peng-Williams Q($\lambda$) update (eq. 7-8)
nodes.statement: $\Delta w_t = \eta\Big[(r_t + \gamma \max_b Q(x_{t+1}, b) - \max_b Q(x_t, b))\, e_t + (r_t + \gamma \max_b Q(x_{t+1}, b) - Q(x_t, a_t))\, \nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)\Big]$, with $e_t = \gamma\lambda\, e_{t-1} + \nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$.

nodes.name: Modified Connectionist Q-Learning (MCQ-L / SARSA)
nodes.statement: Replaces the $\max_b Q(x_{t+1}, b)$ target by $Q(x_{t+1}, a_{t+1})$ for the action actually selected, so temporal-difference errors add up correctly whether or not greedy actions are taken, without zeroing the eligibility trace.
input: State $x_t$, selected action $a_t$, reward $r_t$, next state $x_{t+1}$, next selected action $a_{t+1}$

nodes.name: MCQ-L (SARSA) weight update (eq. 9)
nodes.statement: $\Delta w_t = \eta\, \Delta_t^{\text{MCQ-L}}\, e_t(w)$, with $\Delta_t^{\text{MCQ-L}} = r_t + \gamma\, Q(x_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) - Q(x_t, a_t)$.

nodes.name: MCQ-L expected return (eq. 10)
nodes.statement: $Q(x_t, a_t) = \mathbb{E}\big[r_t + \gamma\, Q(x_{t+1}, a_{t+1})\big]$, the expected return given action probabilities $P(a \mid x)$ used to select actions.

nodes.name: MCQ-L is not true Q-learning under exploration
nodes.statement: MCQ-L is not a true Q-learning algorithm unless the greedy policy is followed: temporal-difference errors do not correct upward for past states. With greedy action selection, MCQ-L collapses to standard Q-learning.

nodes.name: On-line MCQ-L update algorithm
nodes.statement: On-line update for MCQ-L: at each time step, perform the weight update as soon as the next selected action $a_{t+1}$ is known, without storing past state-action pairs.
input: Current state $x_t$, eligibility trace $e_{t-1}$, learning rate $\eta$, decay $\gamma\lambda$

nodes.name: On-line MCQ-L update (eq. 11)
nodes.statement: $\Delta w_t = \eta \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} (\gamma\lambda)^{t-1-k} \big(r_k + \gamma\, Q(x_{k+1}, a_{k+1}) - Q(x_k, a_k)\big)\, \nabla_w Q(x_k, a_k)$.

nodes.name: Combined on-line MCQ-L weight increment (eq. 12)
nodes.statement: $\Delta w_t = \eta\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(\gamma\lambda)^{t-1-k}\big(r_k + \gamma Q(x_{k+1},a_{k+1}) - Q(x_k,a_k)\big)\nabla_w Q(x_k,a_k) - \eta\big(r_t + \gamma Q(x_{t+1},a_{t+1}) - Q(x_t,a_t)\big)\nabla_w Q(x_t,a_t)$. The result is only slightly altered and less efficient than the on-line update for either standard $Q$-learning or MCQ-L.

nodes.name: MCQ-L cumulative weighted error (eq. 13)
nodes.statement: $w_t \leftarrow w_{t-1} + \eta\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(\gamma\lambda)^{t-1-k} \Delta_k\, \nabla_w Q(x_k, a_k)$.

nodes.name: On-line connectionist update algorithm for MCQ-L (Figure 1)
nodes.statement: On-line algorithm: reset eligibilities; loop selecting an action, applying the MCQ-L update with the current and next-selected action's $Q$-values, computing $\nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$, decaying and accumulating the eligibility trace, then performing the action and receiving the reward.

nodes.name: Reset eligibilities
nodes.statement: Reset all eligibilities, $e_0 = 0$.

nodes.name: Select action
nodes.statement: Select action $a_t$ (e.g.\ via Boltzmann exploration over $Q(x_t, \cdot)$).

nodes.name: Compute output gradient
nodes.statement: Calculate $\nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$ with respect to selected action $a_t$ only.

nodes.name: Update eligibility trace
nodes.statement: $e_t = \lambda\gamma\, e_{t-1} + \nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$.

nodes.name: Act and observe reward
nodes.statement: Perform action $a_t$, receive payoff $r_t$.

nodes.name: Loop until trial ends
nodes.statement: If trial has not ended, $t \leftarrow t+1$ and go to step 3.

nodes.name: On-line connectionist update algorithm for Q($\lambda$) (Figure 2)
nodes.statement: On-line implementation of Peng-Williams $Q(\lambda)$ in a connectionist network using two error terms per step: one through the trace and one through the current gradient.

nodes.name: Reset eligibilities
nodes.statement: Reset all eligibilities, $e_0 = 0$.

nodes.name: Select action
nodes.statement: Select action $a_t$.

nodes.name: Two-term weight update
nodes.statement: If $t \neq 0$: $\Delta w_{t-1} = \eta\big[(r_{t-1} + \gamma\max_b Q(x_t, b) - Q(x_{t-1}, a_{t-1}))\, e_{t-1} + (r_{t-1} + \gamma\max_b Q(x_t, b) - \max_b Q(x_{t-1}, b))\, \nabla_w Q(x_{t-1}, a_{t-1})\big]$.

nodes.name: Decay trace
nodes.statement: $e_t = \lambda\gamma\, e_{t-1} + \nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$.

nodes.name: Compute gradient
nodes.statement: Calculate $\nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$ with respect to selected action $a_t$ only.

nodes.name: Act and observe reward
nodes.statement: Perform action $a_t$, receive payoff $r_t$.

nodes.name: Loop until trial ends
nodes.statement: If trial has not ended, $t \leftarrow t+1$ and go to step 3.

nodes.name: Boltzmann (softmax) exploration policy
nodes.statement: Actions are sampled with probabilities $P(a_i \mid x_t) = \frac{\exp(Q(x_t, a_i)/T)}{\sum_b \exp(Q(x_t, b)/T)}$, where $T$ is a temperature parameter that controls randomness. As $T \to 0$, the policy approaches the greedy policy.

nodes.name: Boltzmann action-selection probabilities (eq. 15)
nodes.statement: $P(a_i \mid x_t) = \dfrac{\exp(Q(x_t, a_i)/T)}{\sum_b \exp(Q(x_t, b)/T)}$.

nodes.name: Robot navigation in 2D simulated environment
nodes.statement: A simulated robot must navigate to a goal in a 2D environment while avoiding obstacles, using only range sensors and a single trial-end payoff. Used as testbed for comparing the three update rules.

nodes.name: Reward structure for the navigation task
nodes.statement: Payoffs depend on how the trial ends: $p = 1$ if the robot moves within a small fixed radius of the goal; $p = -0.5 + \exp(-d^2 / 2\sigma^2)$ if the robot crashes at distance $d$ from the goal, where $\sigma$ is one wall length of the square room; $p = -0.5$ if the trial times out (after 200 steps), with a $+0.3$ bonus for not crashing.

nodes.name: Network and input encoding
nodes.statement: The $Q$-function is represented by 9 neural networks (one per available action), each with 23 inputs, 8 hidden nodes and a single output, using sigmoidal activations $\phi(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})$. The 23 inputs are coarse-coded sigmoidal units representing the 5 range sensors, distance to goal, and angle to goal.

nodes.name: Back-propagation gradient computation
nodes.statement: For a feed-forward sigmoidal network with weights $w_{ij}$, the output gradients $\nabla_w Q(x_t, a_t)$ used in the weight updates are computed via standard back-propagation through the layers, treating each output neuron's $Q$-value as the function whose gradient is propagated.
output: Vector of output gradients $\nabla_w Q(x, a)$

nodes.name: Sigmoidal hidden-unit gradient (eq. 16-19)
nodes.statement: For a sigmoidal unit, $\dfrac{\partial o_j}{\partial w_{ij}} = \phi'(\mathrm{net}_j)\, o_i$, with $\phi'(z) = \phi(z)(1 - \phi(z))$; for hidden layers, $\dfrac{\partial o_k}{\partial w_{ij}} = \phi'(\mathrm{net}_k) \sum_j w_{jk}\, \dfrac{\partial o_j}{\partial w_{ij}}$.

nodes.name: Weight update with eligibility per weight (eq. 20)
nodes.statement: $\Delta w_e = \eta\, \Delta_t\, e_e$, with one eligibility $e_e$ stored per weight $w_e$ corresponding to the output of the network for the selected action.

nodes.name: Single eligibility per weight in Q-learning
nodes.statement: In $Q$-learning there is only a single temporal-difference error per step (with respect to the network output that produced the current prediction), so only one eligibility per weight is required, rather than one per output as in the general case.

nodes.name: Empirical comparison: success rates and steps to goal
nodes.statement: Tables 1-3 report success rates (out of 25 robots, average over the last 10{,}000 trials) and average steps to goal for 36 different combinations of $\eta$ and $\lambda$ across the three update rules with backward replay and on-line updating; MCQ-L on-line achieved 24/25 successful robots in 1.5 million updates, compared with 22/25 for $Q(\lambda)$ and 14/25 for standard $Q$-learning.

nodes.name: Effect of the discount factor $\gamma$
nodes.statement: Reducing $\gamma$ to $0.99$ allows the robot to arrive at solutions that reach high final payoffs, but does not use efficient trajectories (the robot is often time-out). Without discounting, the robot fails $2/3$ of the time due to time-outs.

nodes.name: Comparison summary
nodes.statement: On-line updating compared to backward replay consistently performs more successfully over a wider range of training parameters for all 3 update rules. MCQ-L and $Q(\lambda)$ updates lead to faster convergence than standard $Q$-learning, and far faster convergence than the simple one-step Q-learning rule, in this connectionist setting.

nodes.name: No convergence proof for connectionist case
nodes.statement: There is no proof of convergence regarding $TD$- or $Q$-learning algorithms in connectionist systems. Consequently, training methods that are less sensitive to parameter choice are desirable, motivating MCQ-L and on-line updating.

nodes.name: Convergence of Q-learning with function approximation
nodes.statement: No proof yet exists regarding the convergence of $Q$-learning or $TD$-algorithms in connectionist (function-approximating) systems. Further comparative studies on a discrete-state-space problem are needed where preliminary results support the empirical claim that MCQ-L and $Q(\lambda)$ updates lead to faster convergence than standard $Q$-learning.
